articles.title: This Awesome LEGO-Like Original Xbox Building Kit Comes Out Tomorrow
articles.summary: Mattel has announced a LEGO-like building kit for the original Xbox game console in celebration of its 25th anniversary.
articles.body:
In celebration of Xbox’s 25th anniversary, Mattel Brick Shop will release a new LEGO-like building kit based on the original Xbox ( see it at Amazon ). Once assembled, this 3,509-piece set turns into a 1:1 scale model of the game console. It includes the console, a hefty full-size Duke controller, and hidden dioramas for three major Xbox games. It looks great. It's priced at $329.99, with a release date of October 1 (that's tomorrow).

Mattel Brick Shop - Original Xbox Console

Mattel Brick Shop - Microsoft Original Xbox

The console itself looks pretty much just like an original Xbox from 2001. Like like the LEGO Game Boy , the hefty Duke controller has buttons you can press – and when you press them, it triggers interactive lights and sounds in the dioramas hidden inside the console. According to the press release, “Fans can also discover a hidden button combination that triggers an exclusive lighting sequence.” Pretty cool.

The dioramas are worth calling out specifically. Tucked under panels in the console itself are little scenes from three popular Xbox games: Halo: Combat Evolved , The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind , and Psychonauts . (Yes, it's ironic that this is coming out after Microsoft has spun off Psychonauts developer Double Fine Productions). You can keep the dioramas hidden, or you can remove them to display alongside the set.

Additionally, the set comes with 12 “NanoWorld” figures from the games, including Halo’s Master Chief, Psychonauts’ Razputin Aquato, and more.

Formerly known as Mega Bloks, Mattel Brick Shop launched in 2025 as a line of buildable models that come in pieces for you to put together. If that sounds familiar, yes, they’re very similar to LEGO sets . But if the world is big enough for both Coke and Pepsi to co-exist, why not two competing lines of buildable models?

One difference between the two companies is that they’ve courted different brand licenses. LEGO has the likes of Nintendo , Pokémon , Star Wars , and Harry Potter . Mattel, the newer of the two lines, has Masters of the Universe , Hot Wheels , and Xbox. If you’re interested, you can find more Mattel Brick Shop sets here .

Chris Reed is a senior commerce editor and deals expert for IGN. He also runs IGN's board game and LEGO coverage. You can follow him on Bluesky .

articles.title: LEGO PlayStation Is Now Available for LEGO Insiders
articles.summary: LEGO PlayStation is now available for LEGO Insiders, and it comes with a free Astro Bot Set. Here's how to become and Insider for free.
articles.body:
Good news, retro gaming fans: the LEGO set based on the original PlayStation console is now available ( see it at LEGO ). The only catch is that you need to be a LEGO Insider to buy it. Thankfully, you can sign up for free right here . LEGO PlayStation costs $179.99, and it comes with LEGO Astro Bot as a free Gift with Purchase.

If you aren’t a LEGO Insider and you refuse to sign up for a free account for some reason, you’ll be able to buy LEGO PlayStation starting October 4. It’s possible it will sell out quickly, and it’s also possible LEGO Astro Bot will sell out. So if you want to make sure you get one, you’ll want to sign up for the (again, free) LEGO Insiders program .

LEGO PlayStation is a near 1:1 scale set of Sony’s original gaming console, which came out in 1994 in Japan and 1995 in the US. It includes the console as well as the original no-analog-sticks PlayStation controller (the DualShock wouldn’t arrive until three years later).

As with most pricy LEGO sets for adults , the LEGO PS1 has some fun Easter eggs to find. First of all, set's box calls back to the box the original PlayStation came in, which is pretty great. The set's Power and Open buttons actually work. Pressing Power flips a green LEGO piece into view underneath it, as if you were turning it on. The Open button releases the disc cover, letting you see two dioramas hidden inside.

The dioramas are based on Gran Turismo (1997) and Ape Escape (1999). These dioramas can also be removed from the set to display on their own (though that leaves a hole on either side of the PS1 model).

As for LEGO Astro Bot, it's a free Gift With Purchase, but you'll be able to buy it separately at PlayStation Direct for $24.99.

For more about new and future sets, check out all the upcoming LEGO set release dates . And if you want more LEGO sets based on video games, check out our picks for the best Nintendo LEGO sets .

Chris Reed is a senior commerce editor and deals expert for IGN. He also runs IGN's LEGO coverage and maintains the upcoming release dates articles for video games , LEGO sets , and 4K Blu-rays . You can follow him on Bluesky .

articles.title: Florence Pugh’s Netflix Adaptation Has a New Take on the Question of Where Do Monsters Come From
articles.summary: Beautifully shot and dramatically riveting, Netflix's East of Eden, starring Florence Pugh, Christopher Abbott and Mike Faist, is definitely binge-worthy TV.
articles.body:
East of Eden debuts on Netflix on October 1.

Good vs. evil, brotherly rivalries, parental rejection, the notion of free will as opposed to fate… East of Eden has a lot going on. And the new Netflix iteration of the John Steinbeck epic is pretty great at conveying these ideas with a well-acted, handsomely produced, seven-episode miniseries that’s the streaming equivalent of a page-turner.

I confess to having never seen Elia Kazan’s 1955 adaptation of East of Eden in its entirety, despite its status as one of only three starring vehicles for James Dean. But what I do remember about it is mish-mashed in my head with another of his films, Giant, so much so that I was a bit surprised by how this version ended. That may also be in part because, surprisingly, there haven’t been a ton of film or TV adaptations of East of Eden beyond the Kazan/Dean film; there was a TV miniseries in 1981 starring Jane Seymour, and a long-gestating movie version that had Jennifer Lawrence attached at one point but never materialized, but otherwise that’s it.

And that’s just fine, because now Kazan’s granddaughter, the actress Zoe Kazan, has adapted the 1952 novel for the small screen. Along with directors Garth Davis and Laure de Clermont-Tonnerre, Kazan takes the story and imparts a modern sensibility to what is, after all, an age-old tale. For East of Eden makes no bones about its ultimate source, which is the biblical tale of Cain and Abel. Indeed, the very title comes from the Book of Genesis: “So Cain went out from the presence of the Lord and lived in the land of Nod, east of Eden.”

Only in this version of the story, the second Black Widow and the third Professor Xavier star! (Also, a former Ghost Rider villain shows up for a supporting turn.) I’m talking, of course, about Florence Pugh, who really is the centerpiece of this version of the story as Cathy Ames, and Christopher Abbott, who is the second lead as Adam Trask. Mike Faist (Challengers) plays Adam’s brother Charles, who winds up in the middle of things between Cathy and Adam even while the latter two are destined to marry and have children someday. East of Eden is a generational story, as we start Episode 1, “Brothers,” in the post-Civil War Connecticut of 1874 and eventually find our way to California’s Salinas Valley circa World War I in the finale, “Timshel.”

“I believe there are monsters born in this world to human parents,” Pugh’s Cathy tells us in voiceover in the opening line of the series. And that is certainly an idea that lingers over the 46 years or so of the Trask family that we are to bear witness to, though whereas Cathy – a cruel woman who does unspeakable things to those who love her most – takes that notion to be incontrovertible, Kazan is less convinced. Cathy may be a monster, but was she born that way or did other monsters turn the once innocent child that she was into one of their own?

Episode 1 spends a good amount of time with the young versions of Adam (Costa D'Angelo) and his brother Charles (Tom Sweet), as they are forced to run military drills under their father Cyrus (a hateful Tracy Letts), whose heart is still in the war and who plays favorites with his sons. “Adam, don’t you see? I love you better,” Cyrus tells his elder son while Charles is barely within earshot. And yet he has a funny way of showing this affection, choosing to send Adam off to fight in the army while making Charles – the son who actually has an interest in enlisting – stay home to mind the farm.

By the time Cathy comes into the brothers’ lives years later, she’s on death’s doorstep as well as the Trasks’, having been beaten savagely by forces unknown. She will also soon drive a wedge between Adam and Charles, just as their father did, upending all their lives in the years to come, even while that central question will continue to come up: Are monsters born, or are they made?

East of Eden constantly raises this idea, and sometimes it’s a bit too on the nose about it. “I want to be good” and similar lines are uttered by characters who we already know are struggling with the choices they’ve made, or are about to make. But then it has moments of sublime exploration of such notions. In particular, the relationship that forms between Hoon Lee’s Lee and Ciarán Hinds’ Samuel Hamilton yields a philosophical discussion around the idea of “timshel” – a Hebrew word that, according to Steinbeck’s translation, means “thou mayest.” In other words, you may, or you may not. It’s your choice to do good… or bad.

Hoon Lee (Your Friends & Neighbors) is a standout in this series, eventually entering the picture as the Chinese manservant of Adam’s household who, despite being American born, is still treated as a lesser by most of the whites who he lives among. His connection to Adam and Adam’s own sons, and how it leads him to reflect on his own life, is both heartwarming and at times sad. Hinds too plays an important and memorable part in the Trask family as Adam and Cathy move out West, while Joseph Zada and Joe Anders eventually join the series as the years progress, playing twin brothers Caleb and Aron, respectively, and effectively continuing the themes of fraternal friction as 20th century counterparts to their father and uncle.

As for Pugh, Abbott and Faist, the trio are excellent in their roles, with Pugh in particular standing out as the complicated, headstrong, smart, and quite evil Cathy. Though indeed born of human parents as Cathy was, Zoe Kazan’s East of Eden can’t help but contemplate how even a character like this could be the result of more than just fate. “To a monster, the norm must seem monstrous,” Cathy says in that same VO. But what if that monster had no choice but to become monstrous in order to survive?

articles.title: Gears of War: E-Day Missing Classic Features From Original Games
articles.summary: Classic features such as taking enemies hostage as a "meat shield" and duelling with the chainsaw attachments on Lancer assault rifles won't be in Gears of War: E-Day at launch. According to a developer blog from The Coalition, it wasn't possible to build these features out for launch because this prequel was built from scratch, rather than on the bones of previous Gears of War titles.
articles.body:
Classic features such as taking enemies hostage as "meat shields" and dueling with the chainsaw attachments on Lancer assault rifles won't be in Gears of War: E-Day at launch. According to a developer blog from The Coalition , it wasn't possible to build these features out for launch because this prequel was built from scratch, rather than on the bones of previous Gears of War titles.

"We started E-Day with an empty hard drive building our entire gameplay sandbox from scratch to ensure a more unified gameplay experience across Campaign, PVE and PVP," The Coalition said. "This new sandbox also allowed for innovation in cover, combat and enemies. The trade-off being that including every legacy feature from Gears of War was not possible for launch."

The developer said it is working hard to deliver these features, along with Private Lobbies and leaderboards, post-launch or in its next title. If The Coalition makes another one, I hope they call it Gears of War: Bidet.

The Complete Gears of War Timeline (So Far)

E-Day's first Season kicks off with the Early Access release (today at 8am PT / 11am ET) and runs for eight weeks until December 1. The Season includes all launch maps, modes, and cosmetics, as well as three seasonal events: Halloween, 20 Years of Gears, and Thanksgibbing. Ranked modes arrives later, on October 13.

Elsewhere, the blog talks about big changes to the Gnasher, Gears of War's iconic shotgun that turns other players into giblets.

In previous games, hip firing the Gnasher resulted in a blast in whatever direction your character was facing. In E-Day, this system blends camera aiming and muzzle position to give players more control over those last-minute boomstick blasts.

Last month, Xbox laid off a further 268 members of staff , with the story director of E-Day among those cut. In June 2024, Microsoft pledged to continue the story of Gears of War and wrap up the cliffhanger posed by Gears 5's ending, despite creating a prequel first with E-Day.

Whether that still comes to fruition or not likely depends on the success of E-Day, with developers at The Coalition reportedly already concerned they'll face cuts as soon as the upcoming game launches. "It's hard to believe anything they say anymore," a The Coalition developer told Eurogamer.

articles.title: After 'Crunching Hard' Through Their Final Months, Gears of War: E-Day Developers Are Reportedly Now Expecting Layoffs
articles.summary: Gears of War: E-Day developers are reportedly in no mood to celebrate the game's imminent release, following months of overtime and fresh fears of further layoffs.
articles.body:
Gear of War: E-Day developers are reportedly in no mood to celebrate the game's imminent release, following months of overtime and fresh fears of further layoffs.

That's according to a Eurogamer report that includes comments from various sources at The Coalition, Microsoft's dedicated Gears of War team that has been working on E-Day for the past five years.

Microsoft has made numerous rounds of redundancies over that time, though staff at The Coalition say they previously felt somewhat insulated from the job losses due to their work on such a high-profile project. But as their time building Gears of War: E-Day has wound down — a period that has also reportedly seen them "crunching hard" — there are now serious concerns that layoffs may soon be on the horizon for them, too.

The Complete Gears of War Timeline (So Far)

"The mood is certainly 'let's not celebrate the game until we're three months post launch, just in case', which is very unusual," one source said.

"We're just expecting the next wave [of layoffs], or being reorganized under Activision or something later this year," claimed another.

Xbox boss Asha Sharma unveiled a plan to cut 3,200 jobs across the company this year back in July, when the first 1,600 redundancies were announced . Then, last month, a second batch of layoffs were confirmed alongside major structural changes that saw Halo Studios downsized and the franchise handed to Activision, which will also manage veteran British studio Rare . With such seismic changes for Xbox's flagship shooter franchise, suddenly nothing seemed as certain for its Gears of War team.

Staff say they are now "on edge" for the hammer to drop, especially following the "very demoralizing" layoff of Gears of War: E-Day story director Juan Vaca, who was recently culled just two weeks before the game's release.

"I can only imagine the heartbreak of spending all those years on a game to have the final stretch ripped away, completely out of your control," another source said, commented on Vaca's departure. "It's like you planned for a year on a meal for your family where everyone will be there and the day of, you get locked out of the building or something and can't join in."

Microsoft declined to provide an official response to Eurogamer for its report, though it is understood that Microsoft has acknowledged staff have worked hard on getting E-Day out the door, and that this extra effort includes out-of-hours toil that will be repaid in additional holiday.

Xbox is yet to detail when its final round of layoffs this year will take place, though even if The Coalition is told it's safe for now, some staff have suggested they still won't breathe a sight of relief. "It's hard to believe anything [Microsoft leadership] say anymore after discarding staff in this manner," one employee stated.

Tom Phillips is IGN's News Editor. You can reach Tom at tom_phillips@ign.com or find him on Bluesky @tomphillipseg.bsky.social

articles.title: Riftbound Radiance TCG: Exclusive Mordekaiser Card Reveal
articles.summary: Riftbound’s fifth set, Radiance, is coming up soon, so that means new Legends to play around with before the end of the year. We’re happy to exclusively reveal the overnumbered variant for the new legend, Mordekaiser.
articles.body:
Riftbound’s fifth set, Radiance, is coming up soon, so that means new Legends to play around with before the end of the year. We’re happy to exclusively reveal the base and overnumbered variant for the new legend, Mordekaiser.

Mordekaiser, The Iron Revenant, is another new Legend introduced to Riftbound, and this particular variant showcases his original form alongside the spiritual armored form known from the game. His main ability is to add power that can be recycled for any rune or color when playing a unit or gear, as long as it’s possible to banish or remove-from-game a unit or gear card already in the trash.

IGN Exclusive Reveals - Riftbound: League of Legends TCG Radiance

Mordekaiser is also a legend of Fury (red) and Order (yellow), so expect some aggressive play with Deathknell littered about. Having the wild power is nice for color fixing if you don’t have the corresponding rune to recycle, but it’s even more handy for using towards the recycle cost of potential quick draw or ambush cards. Maybe we’ll see more of that leading up to the release of Radiance.

Riftbound Radiance’s English release is set for October 23 with pre-release events starting as early as October 16 at your local game stores. For more Riftbound, check out our hands-on impressions of the last set, Vendetta , and our interview with Riot about the first opposing domain Legends introduced into the game.

Mike Mamon is a Syndication & Digital Specialist at IGN, devil fruit user, and Warrior of Light. Let's chat anime or TCGs on Bluesky @xpmnms.bsky.social

articles.title: Gears of War: E-Day Review
articles.summary: A prequel that returns to the heart of this series.
articles.body:
Editor's Note : This review currently only covers Gears of War: E-Day's story campaign, as that’s all reviewers were given access to ahead of release. It will be updated with a finalized score and multiplayer impressions once we spend some time with the Versus and Horde Siege modes.

To the casual observer, Gears of War has always been a heavy-metal third-person cover shooter about a bunch of meatheads with chainsaws attached to their guns fighting aliens. But what Gears fans know all too well is that the real secret to the series’s two decades of success isn’t the killer graphics, the smart cover mechanics, or the gloriously gratuitous gore – although those things are all certainly significant parts of the recipe. It’s the heart. Marcus and Dom’s brotherhood. JD or Del’s sacrifice (depending on what you chose to do in Gears 5). Dom’s relentless love for Maria. And so my biggest question heading into Gears of War: E-Day, a prequel to the first game set 14 years prior on the day the Locust emerged from underneath the planet Sera, was how it would hang onto that heart when we already knew our armor-clad bros would definitely be alive by the end. I’m thrilled to say that E-Day carries its own satisfying emotional weight, with additional welcomed backstory for Marcus and Dom leading the way – oh, and the action is pretty top-notch, too.

E-Day begins with our Coalition of Ordered Government (COG) heroes, Marcus Fenix and Dominic Santiago, completing a ceremonial tour to honor their service in the finally-ended 79-year Pendulum Wars. We get glimpses of how each of them is reckoning with the end of the only thing they’ve ever known: Marcus is ready to re-enlist and hoping Dom will join him, while Dom is ready to go home to his wife Maria and their two young children, who are growing up without him. Of course, things quickly go to Hell – or rather, Hell comes up to them. Gears of War: E-Day does an excellent job of conveying both the uncertainty and the horror of what’s happening to these characters, even when we as players know exactly what’s going on.

By happenstance, Marcus and Dom get unofficially paired up with ex-Gear Mags Carter and rookie Gear Lucas Reyes, who happen to be at the same bar when the Locust tremors begin, before the quartet officially becomes Bravo Squad once the COG starts organizing its defenses. E-Day deserves a lot of credit here: In a prequel like this where you’re already attached to the leads, it would be easy for Carter and Reyes to be throwaway side characters who exist only to further the stories of our two well-known heroes. But E-Day makes time for your lesser-known Bravo squadmates, dedicating entire meaningful and enjoyable sections to establishing them in this world and getting you to care about them.

The unfolding nightmare of E-Day is reflected in both the types of Locust monsters you face as the campaign progresses as well as the sorts of weapons you’ll need to put them back in the ground. Easily-dispatched Wretches and run-of-the-mill, Hammerburst-wielding Drones are on the front lines as Bravo Squad wonders what the hell it’s up against in the invasion’s opening hours. You’ll take them down with Gears of War staples like the Gnasher shotgun and Lancer, both the bayonet-clad original version and the prototype of the chainsaw-equipped revision. Yes, you’ll get your hands on Gears’s most famous firearm pretty early, and you even get to witness its fun little origin story.

But as you move through the first hours of the Locust invasion, Bravo Squad is continually confused and terrified at the increasingly deadly horrors trying to kill them. The monster menagerie is, naturally, a mix of foes you have and haven’t seen before in other Gears of War games, and the battles get steadily more white-knuckle as you make your way through the five-act story. Giant, frog-like hopping freaks that arc multi-gallon acidic loogies at you. Heavies that come in multiple varieties, most menacingly the one that fires a medium-range Gorehook – a hook on a chain that will typically down you in one hit.

On that note, one of my few complaints about Gears of War: E-Day is related to the down-but-not-out situations you’ll find yourself in throughout the campaign. When, not if, you get downed, your allies will occasionally be standing right next to you and not revive you. In fairness, it wasn’t a constant occurrence, but there were numerous times throughout my 15-18 hour first playthrough when I got stomped to death by a Locust heavy because one of my buddies either stood next to me and didn’t get me up, ran off and left me for dead, or never even got over to me as I mashed the X button to cling to life for a while. The immediate solution for this is to play through E-Day in four-player online co-op (two-player split-screen is the limit on a single Xbox), but I sure hope a patch resolves this inconsistent AI behavior sooner rather than later as well.

As with the Locust enemies, E-Day’s weapons are a mix of old and new, and my goodness do I love them. Every weapon has a unique purpose to suit a particular combat strategy. And man, it still feels awesome to blast a Locust Heavy to bits with the Gnasher shotgun, cut a Drone into pieces with the Lancer Prototype’s chainsaw attachment, or explode a Locust sniper’s head with a scoped-Longshot kill. But there’s so much more in there beyond those Gears classics. The Breechshot, first introduced in the often-forgotten Gears of War: Judgment, ended up being one of my go-tos the longer the campaign went on, as it offered solid range and stopping power without being as cumbersome as something like the Longshot sniper rifle.

But there are a lot of weapons I’d give shoutouts to as well, like the Incinerator, which shotgun-blasts a burst of flesh-melting Imulsion; the Ripper, which is basically the Gears-universe equivalent of a SAW; and the ol’ favorite Torque Bow, which has a hell of a windup but then unleashes an explosive arrow at your target. I loved the weapon complement here, as well as the options that deep roster of firearms afforded me in some of the campaign’s later battles.

And it’s not just that all of these weapons are fun to use in the right situation. They can also all be modified and upgraded through E-Day’s new Weapon Mod and Tactical Gear system. You’ll encounter dozens of yellow Hard Cases lightly hidden throughout the world for you to find. Each contains a mod for one weapon or another, such as accuracy enhancers, scopes, or clip extenders. Completing optional secondary objectives around the major industrial city of Kalona where E-Day takes place also grants these same rewards. Each weapon has four mod slots, which you’ll unlock as you go, and I found myself constantly tweaking each weapon to find the right mix of add-ons that suited my playstyle. As such, I was plenty motivated to find every Hard Case I could and complete every secondary objective possible.

In addition to this is the Tactical Gear that modifies your armor, giving you your choice of a few squad-affecting special abilities that recharge on a cooldown timer after you use them. Again, you’ll unlock more as you progress, but once I got my hands on the Stim that allowed me to heal myself and any teammates within its radius for a short time, I was never tempted by any of the other choices. All of these customization options evolve the classic Gears of War combat in a welcome but not radical way that I appreciate, while liberally placed Supply Caches let you cycle weapons and mods rather frequently if you so choose.

And you’ll be glad for the ability to rearrange your weapon loadout often in E-Day’s mini-boss fights and full-blown boss battles. Almost all of them are memorable in a good way. With, again, a mix of old and new “faces,” these were often barely-scrape-by bouts during my playthrough and ones I welcomed both when they arrived and when I emerged victorious.

E-Day is packed with beautiful locations. The destroyed downtown of Kalona; the pitch-black, Locust-dug caves underneath it; the almost sinister-looking Imulsion refinery; the peaceful mountaintops outside the city. Although the entire campaign doesn’t take place there, you’ll spend a healthy amount of time in Kalona, and the massive but dense battle spaces there are an excellent evolution of the mostly empty open-world areas from Gears 5. The freedom feels far more organic and meaningful here, as there are so many interesting things around almost every corner.

In addition to the aforementioned secondary objectives that grant meaningful Weapon Mod upgrades, there are hidden objects with optionally-viewed details that add a bit of color to a world in the process of recovering from a 79-year civil war, only to be invaded and destroyed by the Locust in a few days. The gorgeous visuals are brought down only by infrequent but noticeable framerate hitches, even while playing in Performance Mode on the Xbox Series X. As such, I can’t recommend playing on the 30fps Quality Mode – at least not before a patch or two.

On a side note, I appreciate that E-Day doesn’t do the all-too-common “make the player run the gauntlet of everything they’ve already fought, but multiply it” endgame sequence. Instead, your mettle is tested plenty of times along the way, with ample quiet moments to punctuate the loud action. And the ending is, I’ll say without spoiling anything, satisfying , which isn’t an easy thing to pull off when, as I mentioned, we already know that Marcus and Dom make it out of E-Day alive. And thank goodness, because I need more quippy Marcus Fenix one-liners in my life; I can’t get enough of them.

By going back to the beginning, Gears of War: E-Day returns to the heart of this series: Marcus Fenix, Dom Santiago, and a Locust horde that’s as terrifying as it is dangerous. E-Day pulls off the tightrope act of giving us a heartfelt prequel with strong characters even when we know how it ends. On a more mechanical level, it also evolves the enemies, weapons, and combat you’d expect to deliver a Gears of War campaign that stands toe-to-toe with any of the others. It wraps up with 10 years still left to go before Marcus gets tossed in prison ahead of the events of the first Gears of War, so here’s hoping the next one stays in the past for a while longer – and that we don’t have to wait another seven years for it to arrive.

articles.title: Gears of War: E-Day is a great game launching at a terrible time
articles.summary: Gears of War: E-Day is a prequel that gets to the core of what makes Gears games great, but it’s launching at a difficult time for Xbox.
articles.body: There are few blockbuster games that are as confident as Gears of War: E-Day. A prequel to one of Xbox’s most transformative titles, E-Day knows exactly what it wants to be: a brutal, tense, and self-aware action game, one that is stronger because it doesn’t deviate from that premise. Twenty years since the original Gears of War, there’s still nothing like its particular brand of up-close cover shooter gameplay, and E-Day shows that it still hits hard two decades later. As Xbox moves into a messy new era focused on its biggest franchises, E-Day could be an early glimpse at the future of the platform. But it’s also launching during one of the most tumultuous periods in Xbox history. Set 14 years before the original Gears, E-Day tells the story of a pivotal point in the franchise’s sci-fi lore: “emergence day,” the moment when an alien collective known as the Locust Horde revealed itself with a surprise attack designed to wipe out the entire human race. You play as a slightly younger, but still gruff and experienced, soldier named Marcus Fenix as he and his squad attempt to fight back against the subterranean extraterrestrials. Marcus is part of an elite group known as “gears,” which are basically really buff guys and gals that wear massive armor and are thrown into action when things get really bad. Things don’t get much worse than the events of E-Day. The human planet Sera is absolutely annihilated by the horde, which launches attacks from holes in the ground and has carved out a labyrinth of underground tunnels that allow them to strike anywhere. Marcus and his squad are thrown into the fray, tasked with doing everything they can to fight back and help where they’re able. Missions have you attacking enemy strongholds, escorting important supply caravans, and searching for survivors amid the rubble. Over the course of the game you see the planet turn from a retrofuturistic paradise to the ruins of a lost civilization. [Media: E-Day is reminiscent of a James Cameron film: Absolutely every element is in service to creating a thrilling sci-fi spectacle. It’s as close to a playable Aliens as you’re bound to find. The cover shooter action remains visceral; everything has a weight to it, from Marcus’ slow movements to the chunky feel of reloading a shotgun. E-Day nails the sense of being pinned down in the middle of a war, surrounded on all sides, being terrified you’ll run out of bullets before the enemy does. There’s an unparalleled sense of tension. E-Day does an excellent job of mixing things up so that you aren’t spending the whole game hiding behind chunks of concrete or burned-out husks of cars. There are huge set-pieces where the world crumbles around you as gigantic aliens lay waste to the city, and eerily quiet moments where you wander through a dark tunnel or foggy cemetery, unsure of what terrors await. E-Day has some side missions, but its world is largely linear, pushing you through one sequence after another with pacing that never really lets up. It’s all rendered with a lavish attention to detail on everything from the way blood splatters on the camera after a particularly gruesome kill to the outline of a leather wallet in the back pocket of Marcus’ jeans as he’s forced into combat in civilian clothes. This conceit also means that, much like Avatar and its sequels, E-Day’s story is to the point and straightforward. Cutscenes give you just enough detail to care about the characters when dramatic things happen, but don’t get in the way of the action. No, the series hasn’t reached the emotion promised by the memorable “Mad World” commercial, but it doesn’t need to. In fact, much of the writing feels intentionally stupid, driving home that this is, at its very core, a dumb action game. The amount of ridiculous one-liners in the game approaches an art form, with pivotal moments punctuated by lines like “A giant floating ballsack with glowing eyes is trying to kill us!” or “Hold on to your dicks!” The true spiritual energy of E-Day can be found in its barks, those lines tossed out by Marcus and his comrades as they mow down alien bad guys. Here are a few examples: * “Too ugly to live.” * “Where are you going? I thought you wanted some of this.” * “Rest in pieces.” * “It ain’t your day, asshole.” * “Looks dead to me.” * “Lights out, fuckface.” * “How do you like that, you stupid-ass spider bitch?” [Image: That’s just a sampling. There’s a strangely joyous nature to the dialogue. The game is violent, the story is dire, but you’re still meant to enjoy the action of firing big guns and using a chainsaw to cut aliens in half. It feels good to play, and the campaign puts you through a range of emotions — at points it even approaches horror, with pitch-black tunnels teeming with bloodthirsty creatures — while never letting go of its action core. E-Day is a 2006 version of Gears rendered with the technology of 2026, which I mean as a total compliment: It’s a pure action game that isn’t saddled by modern trends. It is also launching at an especially challenging time. Xbox is in the midst of “reset,” in which new CEO Asha Sharma is gutting the division, slashing around 3,200 jobs, and dramatically shaping how its current studios operate, with the ultimate — and perhaps unattainable — goal of focusing entirely on Xbox’s biggest franchises to reach a billion players. In a certain light, E-Day is indicative of this new approach, even if it predates Sharma’s time in charge. After launching tentpole franchises like Forza and Halo on the PlayStation 5, E-Day appears to represent a shift back to Xbox console exclusives. In essence, it’s a big, boisterous return for an iconic series, one that you can only play on Microsoft platforms. If you wanted an idea of what the future of Xbox could look like, E-Day offers an enticing vision. I’m not entirely confident that the future will play out like that. Xbox’s strategic plans shift constantly, and E-Day developer The Coalition was hit with at least one layoff before launch, and staff fear more are coming. Xbox’s new leadership says that it wants to “focus on higher priority projects,” which on the surface sounds a lot like a bold, confident return for Gears of War. That’s exactly what you get with E-Day, but it might not be enough for whatever comes next for Xbox. Gears of War: E-Day launches on October 6th on the PC and Xbox.

Grandma’s dinner has to come from somewhere.Grave Mistakes will be available on PC via Steam in November 2026. You can sign up for the playtest on Steam if you're interested.

articles.title: Escape from Playtime Is its Own Uniquely Twisted Multiplayer Toy Story | IGN Preview
articles.summary: And though Escape From Playtime isn’t Mob Entertainment’s first attempt at a multiplayer game, building one inside the Poppy Playtime universe and putting players inside the furry bodies and twisted minds of the monsters of the factory hopes to be their most robust attempt.
articles.body:
Each additional shift you take makes things tougher.

You can’t directly attack; you can only use items to fight back.

You can play solo, but co-op will be the way to go if you can.

Toy Story might be pop culture’sthe most recognizable take on the idea that our toys have a life of their own when we're not around, but Mob Entertainment’s Poppy Playtime might be among the more unique approaches totakes on the concept. It’s story, about shoving sentience into the products in a toy factory and those very abominations rebelling against their creators, is a sort of dark horror that has really spoken to a dedicated and growing audience of fans across games, film, and more. And though Escape From Playtime isn’t the studio’s first attempt at a multiplayer game, building one inside the Poppy Playtime universe and putting players inside the furry bodies and twisted minds of the monsters of the factory hopes to be their most robust attempt.

We got to play a few rounds of the co-op extraction looter ahead of its open playtest starting October 1st, and I found it surprisingly challenging in mostly fun ways despite the finicky controls and abundance of small bugs.

As a person unfamiliar with Poppy Playtime, I found Sr. Comms Manager Tyler Sanchez’s rundown of the lore to be helpful. Lots of attention has been paid to making the environments, enemies, and all the little details in between as accurate and respectful of the world they’ve made and that people have immersed themselves into as possible, as well as leaving breadcrumbs for real lore heads to devour. “The community is VERY passionate about the lore,” he punctuated his summary with. A quick perusal of the subreddit shows this to be true pretty immediately - quite a few of the top threads are people sharing early art or debating the merits of certain interpretations of story morsels.

Once we got split into groups and dropped into the factory, I really appreciated how creepy and also silly all of these things were in motion. Walls and furniture askew and messy and towering over our miniscule bodies. Colorful bits and bobs all covered by jagged shadows or washed with eerie, sickly reds or greens. Our teddy characters, the Smiling Critters, whose namesake mugs curl uncomfortably from ear to ear. Mob’s animation origins really make the macabre merriness stick to you as you watch monsters slink through the darkness in pursuit of you.

QA Manager Jostin Bilyeu’s rundown of the gameflow was pleasantly chaotic and elaborate, but boiled down to a simple goal: our team must scavenge loot from around the factory and return it to Barry, a googly-eyed cart, without being caught and killed by the twisted experiments that roam the building’s corridors. Different bits of loot have different point values and rounds, called shifts here, have minimum point quotas that must be reached before you can leave the factory with the victory and move on to the next shift. Easier said than done, of course.

Grabbing loot is pretty straight forward, but you have a very limited amount of inventory space to keep them in. You really have to be discerning when managing the four slots if you're trying to be efficient. The added wrinkle is that most of the items you’ll find have some sort of utility that can be helpful in navigating the labyrinthian factory, like glow sticks you can mark important features or leave trails with. I got a kick out of the airhorn, which can be useful in helping your teammates find you with the unfortunate downside of also letting the enemy know your approximate location.[

Even when our squad of four had our pockets filled to the brim, we never had enough to hit the threshold in one wave, so we’d have to double back deeper into the factory on the hunt for more valuables. The deeper we ventured, the more the factory itself became its own oppressive enemy. With so many halls and doors that seem to sprawl out endlessly, not to mention the verticality of it all with rooms that potentially go as high as they do wide inviting us to use our ability to climb on practically anything to scour from floor to ceiling. Most of the climbing I did was pretty sketchy, thanks to both my unfamiliarity to the controls and the bugginess that comes with every surface in the game being potentially sticky at the press of a button.

Hazards revealed themselves the deeper we went, like a series of rooms consumed by noxious read CatNap gas, toxic to us if we stayed in it for too long. To clear the gas we had to navigate a path of school room desks whose tops peeked out over the noxious cloud, hopping from desk to desk through a series of rooms in order to pull a series of switches scattered among them. Again, easier said than done, as the floaty jumping could make for some dicey near misses, but I appreciated the way events like this modified the overall task.

And then there’s the other denizens of the dilapidated workhouse that really don’t want you to leave. Of the four enemy types that possibly roam those corridors, I encountered three. Little green Boogie Bots were the bulk of the opponents, rolling around in patrol loops, sounding an alarm when they spotted one of us, and speeding towards us in an attempt to blow us all to bits. The Cat Bees float around like ghosts and latch onto players, and the only way to get them off as they slowly tick your life away is if an ally throws something at them. And then there was Miss Delight, an apparent fan favorite character who wanders the halls almost like a Big Daddy from Bioshock. She is a terrifying threat, and even though my encounter with her was brief - I ran and hid under a box as soon as I got the slightest hint that she was around - the menacing aura was real and palpable.

Monster types are limited, but I didn’t feel like I needed more variety to stay on my toes because each of them are so different and require different strategies to counterplay. I always had to keep a quick exit route in mind for the bots, and was incentivized not to stray too far from the group because of the bees. I also found that, for a game without direct combat (you can only throw your items at enemies and hope for the best), out- maneuvering these foes felt engaging enough that I didn't miss having the option to just simply bash something to death.

When we hit our quota and escaped, we moved on to the next shift, where the necessary number of points to extract raises. And so does the difficulty, as the procedurally generated factory map gets larger, and is filled with a greater variety of environmental hazards and more enemies. The longer you stay in the map looking for loot, the more deadly it gets, as monsters get better at finding you and the poisonous CatNap gas starts to fill the halls of the place. We struggled to stay alive in shift 2 long enough to see how grim it could get, though.

Escape from Playtime has a heavy emphasis on co-op and teamwork, evident in a special room we found that had giant piano keys scattered across it and a song we had to play by pressing the keys in a specific order. Was this puzzle solvable solo? Hell, the whole game can be played in single player, but the pain in the ass it would have been for a little bit of loot and opening a short cut would have made it untenable. That said, the only ways to communicate with other players areis through a single, context-less ping or the proximity voice chat. And without matchmaking, you’ll have to bring your own friends to the party (or I guess join a stranger’s hosted game?), which in its own right could be a challenge as tall as Huggy Wuggy.

Though more challenging than may meet the eye at first, Escape From Playtime’s kleptomaniacal co-op is fun and has a lot of potential. It has steep competition from all sides, as the number of multiplayer games in all genres has explodeds exponentially, but if overnight successes of games like Mecca Chameleon is any indication, small- scope romps with friends can always find a foothold with the right community, and Mob has that in spades.

Enter the factory at your owl peril when Escape From Playtime hits Early Access on Oct 21st.

While you're here, check out these recent previews of other big upcoming games we've checked out recently!

Jarrett Green is a frequent contributor to IGN. Talk video games with him on X/Twitter at @Jarrettjawn .

articles.title: Gears of War E-Day Review, Gameplay Impressions, Videos and Top Features
articles.summary: Gears of War: E-Day from developers The Coalition and People Can Fly hopes to look back to move the iconic series forward.
articles.body:
Gears of War: E-Day from developers The Coalition and People Can Fly hopes to look back to move the iconic series forward.

The first mainline entry in the Gears of War series since Gears 5 in 2019, E-Day is a prequel that finally gives players the chance to experience the fabled Emergence Day, marking the arrival of the Locust Horde.

Promising enhanced cover-based combat, a heartfelt tale with the tried-and-true characters and the necessary multiplayer elements, E-Day hopes for a triumphant return that gets the series back up there with the greats for a new generation.

Another visual feast from Unreal Engine 5, E-Day goes to great lengths to finally deliver the oft-requested environmental damage and outright destruction that fits the Gears series so well.

The battlefields found throughout the game crumble and deform in response to the action in ways that make sense. Beyond just being fantastic-looking and immersive, it adds a fun layer atop the action.

It should go without saying at this point, but overall, the game just looks great in terms of character and environments. The gritty world and expected superb sound effects are nearly unmatched for the chainsaw, overall gunplay and battlefield cries.

This is one of the more gnarly and grisly games out there, even for a series like Gears. Localized damage on an enemy's body will produce some winces, never mind the smattering of gore all over the place by the end of a battle.

Gameplay is oh-so Gears in that great, over-the-shoulder, third-person carnage sort of way.

To accommodate some of the big fluidity changes, E-Day marks the first big control mapping changes in a long time, too. Running is now tied to the left stick, while cover is the "a" face button, to note a few of the big changes. There's an adjustment period, for sure, but it feels better in tandem with the speed of things and options available.

The expansion of mobility just feels right. Players can now slide, take lower cover than normal and climb higher, to name a few options.

This is still very much a love letter to weaponry, too. The active-reload system triumphantly returns in a way only Gears can get right. And players have the option to interrupt a shell-by-shell reload to melee or otherwise react to enemies.

Like past games, the mixture of varied enemies and locales on top of the almost addicting gameplay loop, made all the better by that great-feeling reloading system, makes for a great time. It's still impressive even all these years later that Gears found a way to make "downtime" in a fight while reloading super compelling and important.

Set 14 years before the events of the first game, players link back up with Marcus Fenix and Dominic Santiago to experience the true E-Day on the planet Sera.

It's compelling to actually see the aftermath of the oft-talked-about Pendulum Wars, which features Coalition of Ordered Governments (COG) soldiers like Marcus simply leading normal lives before being ripped into battle with the Locust Horde.

Along those same lines, E-Day manages to recapture the sense of brotherhood amongst its cast that newer games seemed to lose.

We're not going to say it matches the history-making "Mad World" trailer , but it's probably the closest the series has come since.

To its credit, E-Day's campaign mixes it up well. There are linear missions, but also semi-open-world sections that let players run off to explore, tackle side quests and other fun stuff.

This campaign supports four-player online co-op, so it's got that Xbox 360 vibe in terms of linking up with friends.

On the multiplayer side, E-Day hits the expected stuff really well.

There's the four-on-four competitive mode, spanning the classic team deathmatch and conquest modes.

Arena shooters like this require careful balance and it feels good here out of the gates. Players spawn onto a map with the basics like the lancer, shotgun and a smoke grenade, with pre-set spawns of weapons scattered across the map.

Gears nailed this down years ago. Map control of key areas, encouraged by not just cover, but the obtainable weapons, makes for compelling engagements.

For those who want less competition and more collaboration, E-Day also offers Horde Siege, a 12-player co-op mode, with players split into three squads of four. Players pick from one of four classes:

Those squads populate different parts of a bigger map and pursue their own objectives. But it also makes for some really interesting larger-scale events where multiple squad events can come together to survive.

There's a solid progression system of its own within Horde Siege, where difficulty scales with class level and things like energy can be spent on upgrades. There's also a squad perks system to engage with, while survival via extraction is key to keeping some of the goodies.

Overall, Horde Siege is a really fun mixture of good traits from the likes of Helldivers and other extraction greats of the last few years, but with that Gears flair nobody else can match.

E-Day runs well despite some of the really impressive stuff going on and comes with the expected gamut of options for players to tweak.

E-Day nails the most critical items in a new Gears release: Refinements to the combat system that keep it standing alone on the market in the best possible way, with some serious storytelling and character chops.

It's hard to undersell these points. The camaraderie in the face of a world-ending threat the early games achieved so well is finally back. And the seamless cover-based combat with sometimes as simple as reloading being an interesting, strategy-filled action, truly has no equal.

We'll see if Gears as a whole enjoys a resurgence capable of swinging console wars and the like. But for the long faithful and newcomer alike, E-Day easily tops some of the recent releases in the series and is one of the top games of a stacked 2026.

articles.title: La San Diego Comic-Con también es juegos de mesa: One Piece, Star Wars, El Señor de los Anillos y otros grandes se presentan en Málaga
articles.standfirst: Durante el evento podremos probar, muchos de ellos en primicia, distintos juegos de mesa basados en algunos de los universos y franquicias más potentes del mundo.
articles.summary: Durante el evento podremos probar, muchos de ellos en primicia, distintos juegos de mesa basados en algunos de los universos y franquicias más potentes del mundo.
articles.body: La San Diego Comic-Con de Málaga ya está aquí. La que dice ser una de las ferias geek más grandes del mundo ha regresado con un buen puñado de actividades entre las que destacamos —como buenos amantes del género que somos— los juegos de mesa. En efecto. Además de series, videojuegos y cómics, en la San Diego Comic-Con de Málaga podremos disfrutar de un repertorio bastante amplio de juegos de mesa, con algunos de los más conocidos del panorama internacional... así como varias exclusivas. En esta edición ha sido Asmodee la que se ha ocupado de brindarnos esta posibilidad. La editora, presente en la convención del 1 al 4 de octubre, contará con diferentes propuestas en el Palacio de Ferias y Congresos de Málaga (FYCMA). Star Wars, One Piece, El Señor de los Anillos, Marvel, Disney... Hay de todo. Uno de los grandes protagonistas del evento será, sin duda, J.R.R. Tolkien. El autor de ESDLA estará bien representado con pruebas gratuitas de distintos juegos de mesa de la franquicia. Entre ellos encontramos El Señor de los Anillos: Enfrentamiento y El Señor de los Anillos: Círculo de conflicto, que estarán disponibles en exclusiva durante el evento. A ellos se sumarán otros títulos ya conocidos dentro de la franquicia, como La Comunidad del Anillo: El juego de bazas, El Hobbit: Historia de una Ida y de una Vuelta y Duelo por la Tierra Media. Asimismo, también tendremos espacio para descubrir Hellbreak, un nuevo TCG (juego de cartas) de terror que podrá probarse durante el evento antes de su llegada al público. Pero si no eres muy de Tolkien, o te apetece probar otras cosas, pues no te preocupes, porque hay otras opciones. A título personal no puedo evitar destacar One Piece, y es que adoro la obra de Eiichiro Oda en todas sus formas. Y sí, estará presente, ya que también se pueden probar los juegos de mesa de Dobble One Piece y 5 Minute One Piece, dos títulos de los que ya os hemos hablado con anterioridad en otras ocasiones. Hay más. De los piratas más famosos más allá del Grand Line saltamos al espacio exterior con Star Wars, que contará con propuestas como Star Wars: La batalla de Hoth y Star Wars Super Teams. No obstante, si de lo que de verdad tienes ganas es de matar la espera de Doomsday, ojito, porque habrá bastante Marvel en el evento. Juegos de mesa como Dobble Spider-Man y Marvel Champions también estarán presentes, mientras que los personajes de Disney llegarán con Dixit Disney y ¡Qué Desbarate Olaf!. Este último también tendrá su estreno dentro del evento. La oferta no se limitará a estas franquicias. Los asistentes también podrán descubrir las Cartas Coleccionables Kayou, centradas en diferentes universos del anime y la cultura pop, con colecciones inspiradas en Naruto, Guerreras Kpop, Tokidoki y My Little Pony. Uno de los momentos destacados del estand llegará este mismo jueves 1 de octubre, cuando el reconocido autor de juegos Reiner Knizia estará presente para firmar algunos de sus trabajos. Autor de títulos como Modern Art o MLEM, estará firmando autógrafos al tiempo que tienen lugar distintos stands también a cargo de Asmodee. Quienes lo quieran, pueden iniciarse en talleres de aprende a jugar o probar distintos juegos de mesa como Whirly Derby, LEGO Ninjago, DNUP, Exploding Kittens y Los fantasmas no saben dibujar. La programación se completará con propuestas como JinxO, Panda Panda, Cocteleros traicioneros y Rainbow, ampliando todavía más la selección disponible en el estand.
